doctrines/atonement/question: What did Christ’s death accomplish, and how does it reconcile God and humanity?
doctrines/atonement/summary: The creeds confess that Christ was crucified "for us and for our salvation" but never defined how the cross saves. Ransom, recapitulation, satisfaction, moral influence, penal substitution, governmental, Christus Victor, mimetic, nonviolent and participatory models each take up different biblical images and different accounts of the human plight.
doctrines/atonement/longText:
Unlike the Trinity or the person of Christ, the work of Christ was never defined by an ecumenical council. The Nicene Creed says only that he was crucified "for us" and "for our salvation". The New Testament offers a rich cluster of images — ransom (Mark 10:45), sacrifice and the Day of Atonement (Hebrews), propitiation or expiation (Romans 3:25), curse-bearing (Galatians 3:13), victory over the powers (Colossians 2:15), reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5) and example (1 Peter 2:21) — and later theology organised them into "theories" or "models".

The early church spoke above all of victory, healing and participation. Irenaeus saw Christ "recapitulating" Adam’s story and redeeming captives; Athanasius saw the incorruptible Word abolishing death in the body he assumed; Origen and Gregory of Nyssa described a ransom paid to, or a fish-hook concealed from, the devil — imagery that Gregory of Nazianzus and John of Damascus qualified. The Orthodox Easter hymn "trampling down death by death" still carries this vision.

In 1098 Anselm’s Cur Deus Homo reframed the question in terms of God’s honour: sinful humanity owes a satisfaction it cannot pay, so a God-man must pay it. Abelard answered that the cross saves by revealing and kindling love, and was condemned at Sens (1141). The Reformers sharpened satisfaction into penal substitution: Christ bore the penalty of God’s law and the curse due to sinners, and his righteousness is imputed to believers. Socinus denied that satisfaction and forgiveness are compatible; Grotius answered with a "governmental" theory; Owen and the Synod of Dort argued for a definite atonement for the elect, while Amyraldians, Arminians and Wesleyans held that Christ died for all.

In the 19th and 20th centuries John McLeod Campbell re-centred atonement on Christ’s filial response to the Father in our humanity, a line developed by T. F. and J. B. Torrance; Gustaf Aulén’s Christus Victor (1930) revived the "classic" victory model; René Girard’s mimetic theory read the cross as unmasking scapegoat violence; and feminist, womanist and Anabaptist critics proposed nonviolent models. Evangelicals have vigorously defended penal substitution (Packer, Stott, Pierced for Our Transgressions), while many theologians now speak of complementary models within a "kaleidoscope". The "legal vs union" comparison traces how these choices shape whole frameworks of the gospel.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/0/label: What did Christ’s death accomplish — and how does it reconcile God and humanity?
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/0/text: The New Testament uses many images: ransom, sacrifice, propitiation/expiation, victory over powers, reconciliation, example, new creation. No ecumenical council ever defined a single theory of the atonement, so "models" multiplied, each emphasising different texts and a different account of the human plight.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/1/text: "He was wounded for our transgressions … the chastisement of our peace was upon him … the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all." Central to substitutionary readings; also read as solidarity and vindication.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/2/label: Leviticus 16; Hebrews 9-10 — the Day of Atonement
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/2/text: The sacrificed goat and the "scapegoat" bearing Israel’s sins into the wilderness; Hebrews presents Christ as high priest and once-for-all sacrifice. Read sacrificially, penally, or (Girard) as exposing the scapegoat mechanism.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/3/label: Mark 10:45; 1 Timothy 2:6 — a ransom for many
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/3/text: "The Son of man came … to give his life a ransom for many." The root of the patristic ransom motif.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/4/text: Christ "set forth to be a propitiation (hilastērion)"; God "made him to be sin for us"; Christ "made a curse for us". Key texts of satisfaction and penal substitution — and of participation: "one died for all, therefore all died."
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/5/text: Christ "spoiled principalities and powers … triumphing over them"; through death he destroyed "him that had the power of death". The Christus Victor texts.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/6/text: "Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example"; "herein is love … that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation". Texts of moral influence and of love as the source of atonement.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/7/text: Christ sums up and reverses Adam’s story — obedient at a tree where Adam disobeyed — and redeems captives "in a manner consonant to reason".
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/8/label: Athanasius: death abolished in the Lord’s body
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/8/text: The incorruptible Word takes a mortal body so that the death of all is accomplished in him and corruption is undone from within.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/9/label: Origen: the ransom paid to the evil one
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/9/text: Origen reads Mark 10:45 literally: the ransom was paid to the devil, who could not hold the soul of Jesus.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/10/label: Gregory of Nyssa: the divine fish-hook
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/10/text: The devil swallows the bait of Christ’s flesh and is caught by the hook of his divinity.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/11/label: Gregory of Nazianzus: to whom was the ransom paid?
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/11/text: Gregory rejects payment to the devil as outrageous, and payment demanded by the Father as unworthy; he stresses healing by assumption.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/12/text: Humanity is held captive by the devil; Christ’s death is the price or the bait that frees us.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/13/text: Christ re-lives and heals the whole human story, undoing Adam’s disobedience.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/14/text: Sin robs God of honour; only a God-man can repay; Christ’s free death merits a reward passed to us.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/15/text: The cross reveals God’s love and awakens responsive love that frees us from sin.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/16/text: Bernard charges that Abelard leaves Christ a mere example and denies real redemption from the devil’s power.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/17/text: Propositions drawn from Abelard (including on redemption) are condemned and Innocent II confirms; satisfaction thinking, refined by Aquinas, becomes the medieval norm.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/18/label: Late-medieval devotion to the suffering Christ
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/18/text: Satisfaction and merit language shapes Western piety: the realistic crucifix, the Stations of the Cross, indulgences drawn on Christ’s superabundant merits — contrasting with the victorious Christ of Eastern icons.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/19/text: Christ bears in our place the penalty of God’s law and the curse of sin; his righteousness is imputed to us.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/20/label: Socinus: satisfaction and forgiveness are incompatible
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/20/text: If the debt is paid, it is not forgiven; the Polish Brethren reject satisfaction altogether.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/21/text: God as ruler upholds moral order by a public display of what sin deserves, then pardons.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/22/label: Dort (1619) and Westminster (1646): definite atonement, satisfaction of justice
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/22/text: Reformed confessions declare Christ’s death "sufficient for all, efficient for the elect" (Dort II) and that he "fully satisfied the justice of his Father" (WCF 8.5).
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/23/label: General Assembly deposes John McLeod Campbell (1831)
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/23/text: The Church of Scotland deposes Campbell for teaching that Christ died for all and that assurance belongs to faith; his later Nature of the Atonement (1856) reframes atonement filially.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/24/text: Atonement happens in Christ’s whole vicarious humanity: he includes us, confesses, repents, obeys and offers us to the Father.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/25/label: Penal substitution in evangelical preaching and hymnody
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/25/text: From the Evangelical Revival to Hodge, Spurgeon and Billy Graham, penal substitution becomes the heart of evangelical proclamation and assurance.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/26/text: The "classic" view: God in Christ conquers sin, death and the devil.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/27/text: The cross exposes and ends the violent scapegoat mechanism on which cultures are built.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/28/text: Critics such as Joanne Carlson Brown and Rebecca Parker (1989) and Delores Williams (1993) ask whether atonement theories sanctify suffering and violence ("divine child abuse").
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/29/text: Narrative Christus Victor without a God who requires violence.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/30/text: After Steve Chalke’s Lost Message of Jesus (2003) provoked controversy in British evangelicalism, Pierced for Our Transgressions (2007) and others restate penal substitution as Trinitarian self-giving, not abuse.
doctrines/atonement/flow/nodes/31/text: Orthodox churches emphasise victory and theosis (the paschal "trampling down death by death"); Catholic teaching speaks of sacrifice, satisfaction and merit (Catechism 599-618); confessional Reformed, Lutheran and many evangelical bodies treat penal substitution as central; many scholars favour a "kaleidoscopic" plurality of models, while Christus Victor, participatory and nonviolent models are widely revived.
doctrines/church-sacraments/question: What is the Church, who leads it, and what happens in its sacraments?
doctrines/church-sacraments/summary: Christians agree that Christ founded a Church and gave it baptism and the Supper, but have divided over how Christ is present in the Eucharist, how many sacraments there are, whether bishops in apostolic succession are essential, how churches should be governed, whether an unworthy minister invalidates a sacrament, and whether women may be ordained.
doctrines/church-sacraments/longText:
The earliest Christian sources already show a Church gathered around the apostles’ teaching, the breaking of bread and prayer (Acts 2:42), led by overseers, elders and deacons. By about 107 Ignatius of Antioch describes a single bishop with presbyters and deacons in each city and calls the Eucharist "the flesh of our Saviour"; Justin (c.155) says the consecrated food is "not common bread"; Irenaeus (c.180) points to public successions of bishops as the guarantee of apostolic teaching. These three convictions (an apostolic ministry, a realist Eucharist and a visible catholic unity) shaped the Church of the first millennium, East and West.

Crises refined them. After the Diocletian persecution the Donatist schism in North Africa asked whether unworthy clergy could give valid sacraments; Augustine answered that Christ himself baptises and that the Church is a mixed body until the end, establishing the Western doctrine of sacramental validity. In the 9th and 11th centuries Western theologians debated how the Eucharist is Christ’s body; the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) adopted the term "transubstantiation", Thomas Aquinas gave it Aristotelian precision, and the number of sacraments was fixed at seven. The Eastern churches, Chalcedonian and non-Chalcedonian, likewise counted seven mysteries (with East Syriac variations) and affirmed a real change of the gifts by the Spirit, while declining to define its mode.

The Reformation broke this consensus. Luther reduced the sacraments to two and rejected transubstantiation and the sacrifice of the Mass, yet insisted on Christ’s bodily presence "in, with and under" the bread. Zwingli read "is" as "signifies"; the failure of the Marburg Colloquy (1529) divided Lutheran and Reformed Protestants for four centuries, and Calvin’s doctrine of a spiritual real presence became the Reformed standard. Trent reaffirmed seven sacraments and transubstantiation. Questions of church government followed: episcopal, presbyterian and congregational polities each claimed biblical warrant, with consequences for politics and religious liberty from Scotland to New England.

In the modern era the ecumenical movement produced significant convergence (the Leuenberg Agreement of 1973, the WCC’s Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry of 1982, and Rome’s recognition in 2001 of the ancient East Syriac Anaphora of Addai and Mari), while the ordination of women became a new dividing line: practised by Quakers, Holiness and Pentecostal churches, Methodists and most mainline Protestants and many Anglicans, but rejected by the Catholic and Orthodox churches and by complementarian evangelicals. This section presents each view in its own terms, the objections each faces and the replies its defenders make.
doctrines/church-sacraments/flow/nodes/0: What is the Church, who leads it, and what happens in its sacraments?

Jesus gathered disciples, appointed apostles, commanded baptism and said over bread and wine "this is my body ... this is my blood". How is Christ present in the Supper? How many sacraments are there, and are they means of grace or signs of obedience? Who has authority to ordain and preside, and through what form of government? Can an unworthy minister invalidate a sacrament? May women be ordained?
doctrines/church-sacraments/flow/nodes/1: Words of institution and the bread of life (Mark 14:22–24; John 6:48–63)

"Take, eat: this is my body"; "except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you" (John 6:53); yet "it is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing" (6:63). Realists and symbolists both appeal to these texts.
doctrines/church-sacraments/flow/nodes/2: Matthew 16:18–19: "upon this rock I will build my church"

Read as founding Petrine primacy and apostolic succession (Catholic), as Peter’s confession of faith (most Protestants and many Fathers), or as the foundation shared by all bishops (Cyprian, Orthodox).
doctrines/church-sacraments/flow/nodes/3: "The cup of blessing ... is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?"; whoever eats "unworthily" is "guilty of the body and blood of the Lord", "not discerning the Lord’s body".
doctrines/church-sacraments/flow/nodes/4: Offices and ministries (Acts 6; 14:23; Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 2–3; Titus 1; Romans 16:1–7; Galatians 3:28)

Overseers (episkopoi), elders (presbyteroi) and deacons, with "bishop" and "elder" used interchangeably in some texts (Titus 1:5–7); Phoebe a deacon, Junia "of note among the apostles"; but also "I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority" (1 Tim 2:12). Dates of the Pastorals are debated (c.62–100).
doctrines/church-sacraments/flow/nodes/5: Clement of Rome: apostles appointed successors (c.96)
Rome tells Corinth that the apostles appointed bishops and deacons and provided for their succession, so deposing them is wrong.
doctrines/church-sacraments/flow/nodes/6: Ignatius of Antioch: bishop, Eucharist and "the Catholic Church" (c.107)
A single bishop with presbyters and deacons is the focus of unity; the Eucharist is the flesh of Christ.
doctrines/church-sacraments/flow/nodes/7: Earliest description of the Sunday Eucharist, with a realist understanding of the consecrated food.
doctrines/church-sacraments/flow/nodes/8: Irenaeus: succession of bishops guarantees apostolic teaching (c.180)
Against Gnostic secret traditions, public lists of bishops show where apostolic doctrine is found.
doctrines/church-sacraments/flow/nodes/9: Bishops in continuous succession from the apostles guard faith and sacraments; the threefold ministry of bishops, priests and deacons becomes universal by c.200.
doctrines/church-sacraments/flow/nodes/1: Cyprian: no salvation outside the Church; rebaptise schismatics (c.251)
Cyprian’s view that sacraments outside the one Church are void becomes the root of Donatist theology.
Donatism: a pure Church and pure ministers
North Africans reject Caecilian of Carthage because a bishop who consecrated him was accused of handing over Scriptures in persecution; sacraments of traitor clergy are invalid.
Augustine: Christ is the true minister (c.400–416)
Sacraments belong to Christ, not the minister; the visible Church is a mixed body until the harvest.
Conference of Carthage rules against the Donatists (411)
Before the imperial commissioner Marcellinus, 286 Catholic and 284 Donatist bishops debate; the verdict for the Catholics is followed by coercive imperial laws, which Augustine reluctantly defended.
John of Damascus: "not merely figures" (c.743)
The Greek tradition affirms a real change of the gifts by the Holy Spirit at the epiclesis without philosophical definition.
Orthodox eucharistic mystery
Eastern, Oriental and East Syriac churches affirm the real change (metabolē) of the gifts into Christ’s body and blood as a mystery, centred on the Spirit’s descent.
Paschasius vs Ratramnus at Corbie (831–843)

Paschasius Radbertus identifies the eucharistic body with the historical body born of Mary; Ratramnus distinguishes Christ’s body "in figure" from his historical body. Berengar of Tours (d.1088) later revives Ratramnus and is forced to recant (1059, 1079).
Seven sacraments
Peter Lombard’s Sentences (c.1150) fixes the number at seven: baptism, confirmation, Eucharist, penance, anointing, orders, marriage.
Fourth Lateran Council: "transubstantiated" (1215)

Canon 1 confesses that Christ’s body and blood are truly contained under the species of bread and wine, "the bread being transubstantiated into the body"; annual confession and Easter communion are made obligatory.
Transubstantiation
Thomas Aquinas explains that the whole substance of bread and wine becomes Christ’s body and blood while the accidents (appearances) remain.
doctrines/church-sacraments/flow/nodes/2: Florence’s Decree for the Armenians: seven sacraments (1439)
The union council lists seven sacraments with matter, form and minister, building on the profession of Michael VIII at Lyon (1274).
Luther, The Babylonian Captivity of the Church (1520)
Only rites with Christ’s command and promise and a visible sign are sacraments; Luther attacks the withheld cup, transubstantiation as philosophy and the Mass as sacrifice.
Two sacraments (or ordinances)
Baptism and the Lord’s Supper alone are dominical sacraments; Anabaptists and later Baptists call them "ordinances" of obedience.
Zwinglian memorial view
"Is" means "signifies"; the Supper is a commemoration and public confession of faith.
Lutheran sacramental union
Christ’s true body and blood are present "in, with and under" the bread and wine and received by all communicants.
Marburg Colloquy fails on the Supper (1529)

Philip of Hesse brings Luther and Zwingli together to build a Protestant alliance; they agree on fourteen and a half of fifteen articles, but not on the bodily presence. Luther refuses Zwingli’s hand of fellowship.
Lutheran and Reformed churches go separate ways
Separate confessions (Augsburg 1530; Tetrapolitan 1530; Zwingli’s Fidei Ratio 1530), no common military alliance, and centuries of mutual non-communion; Zwingli dies at Kappel (1531).
Reformed spiritual presence
Calvin: believers truly feed on Christ’s body and blood, as the Spirit lifts them to the ascended Christ; Consensus Tigurinus (1549) with Bullinger.
Council of Trent defines transubstantiation and seven sacraments (1547–63)

Session 7 (1547) anathematises denial of seven sacraments; Session 13 (1551) calls the change of substance "fittingly and properly" transubstantiation; Session 22 (1562) defines the Mass as a propitiatory sacrifice; Session 23 (1563) defends priesthood and hierarchy.
Presbyterian and congregational polities

Calvin’s four offices (1541) and the Scottish Books of Discipline (1560, 1578) establish government by elders in graded courts; English Separatists (Robert Browne, 1582) and the Cambridge Platform (1648) set out congregational autonomy, later adopted by Baptists.
doctrines/church-sacraments/flow/nodes/3: Presbyterian majority, Independent (congregationalist) "dissenting brethren" and Erastians clash; the Form of Presbyterial Church-Government (1645) shapes world Presbyterianism; episcopacy is restored in England in 1660.
From Quaker women preachers and Antoinette Brown’s Congregationalist ordination (1853) to Holiness and Pentecostal women evangelists and Florence Li Tim-Oi’s Anglican priesthood (1944).

Catholic (Inter Insigniores 1976; Ordinatio Sacerdotalis 1994) and Orthodox teaching, with complementarian evangelicals (Danvers Statement 1987), hold that presbyteral or pastoral office belongs to men.
Convergence: Leuenberg (1973), BEM (1982), Addai and Mari (2001)

Lutheran and Reformed churches in Europe declare pulpit and altar fellowship (Leuenberg, 1973); the WCC’s Lima text Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry (1982) records wide convergence; Rome recognises the validity of the Assyrian Church of the East’s anaphora of Addai and Mari, which lacks the words of institution (2001); Lutheran–Anglican Porvoo (1992) and Called to Common Mission (1999) share the historic episcopate.

Catholics, Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox and the Church of the East (together well over half of all Christians) hold seven sacraments, a real change of the elements and episcopal succession, and ordain only men as priests. Lutherans hold sacramental union; Reformed and Anglicans a spiritual real presence; most Baptists, evangelicals and Pentecostals a memorial view of two ordinances, usually with congregational or elder-led polity. Women are ordained in most mainline Protestant, Anglican (in many provinces), Methodist and many Pentecostal churches, but not in Catholic, Orthodox, Southern Baptist, LCMS or many conservative evangelical bodies.
